rationale: The plasma samples were run in two acquisition batches, and batch effects in DIA intensities are often as large as the disease signal. I'm adding per-batch mean-centring of each protein, with batch means estimated only on the training fold and then subtracted from the test samples, so the logistic model learns disease differences instead of batch offsets. I haven't run this yet. If batch happens to line up with diagnosis, centring could also remove some real signal, and the dev score will show whether that happens.

The current model only sees proteins quantified in at least 70% of samples. That drops low-abundance proteins, such as brain-derived or inflammatory proteins near the detection limit, whose missingness depends on abundance and may itself carry disease signal. I'm adding binary detected/not-detected indicators for proteins quantified in 20–80% of the training fold. The indicators get the same per-batch centring as the intensities, so the model can't use differences in detection rate between batches. They are joined to the existing intensity features in the same L2 logistic regression.

With only about 70 training samples and about 1,500 retained proteins, most of the L2 weight goes to noise proteins. Only a few hundred plasma proteins (acute-phase, complement and lipid-transport proteins) are expected to carry AD signal. So inside each training fold, after batch centring and imputation, I keep only the 300 proteins with the largest absolute Welch t-statistic and then fit the same L2 logistic regression; this hasn't been run yet, so I don't know if the dev score improves.

Right now each sample is normalized by the median of every protein quantified in it. In plasma DIA, how many low-abundance proteins get quantified changes with sample depth, so a deeper sample has a lower median and all its proteins shift by an artificial offset. I'll compute the median from a fixed reference set instead: the proteins quantified in at least 95% of all samples (chosen without labels). That way the scaling factor reflects loading differences rather than detection depth. I haven't run this, so I don't know the effect on the dev score yet.

Plasma DIA intensities have heavy tails: interference spikes, haemolysis or lipaemia outliers, and extreme half-minimum imputed values. With about 70 training samples, a few extreme standardized values can dominate the L2 logistic fit. This change clips each protein's standardized value to ±3 (bounds set by the training-fold scaler) so that consistent shifts across many samples drive the model rather than single outlier measurements. It has not been run yet.

The current batch correction only shifts each batch's mean. DIA acquisition batches also differ in dynamic range and noise for each protein (for example, from changes in ion-injection or chromatography), so one batch's proteins can dominate the standardized features. I'm switching to a ComBat-like location-scale correction: each batch's per-protein SD is estimated on the training fold, shrunk toward the pooled SD (prior weight 10 samples) because each batch is small, and each batch is rescaled to the pooled SD. I haven't run this, so I don't know the effect on the dev score yet.

Plasma proteomes are strongly affected by pre-analytical contamination: haemolysis releases erythrocyte proteins, and platelet activation releases platelet proteins (Geyer et al. 2019 contamination panels). These shifts vary by sample and spread across hundreds of co-varying proteins, so they can hide the AD signal. This change builds label-free erythrocyte and platelet contamination scores from the panel proteins. It then regresses those scores out of every protein, with coefficients fit on the training fold only, before the L2 logistic regression. Coagulation proteins are left out of the panels because fibrinogen may itself be linked to AD. I haven't run this yet, so I don't know its effect on the dev score.

The number of proteins quantified per sample varies with each sample's quality and instrument sensitivity. It feeds into the features in two ways: the median used to normalise each sample depends on which low-abundance proteins were detected (round 4 showed the normalisation is sensitive to this), and it decides how many values get half-minimum imputation. Contamination regression helped a lot (+0.034), so technical variation is clearly hiding the AD signal. I'm adding detection depth as one more technical covariate, computed without labels as each sample's quantified fraction over all protein groups. It is regressed out of every protein together with the erythrocyte and platelet scores, using coefficients fit on the training fold only.

Each person's immunoglobulin repertoire varies a lot. In undepleted Astral plasma that shows up as a large block of correlated IGHV/IGKV/IGLV/constant-chain protein groups that has nothing to do with AD, and it also distorts the median normalisation. I'm adding a label-free immunoglobulin score, built from proteins by gene-name prefix, as a third nuisance covariate. It is regressed out of every protein together with the erythrocyte, platelet and detection-depth covariates, using coefficients fit on the training fold only. I haven't run it, so I don't know whether the dev score improves.

I'm lowering the protein-retention threshold from ≥70% to ≥50% quantified in the training fold. This brings in lower-abundance plasma proteins near the detection limit, where leakage-derived brain proteins and inflammatory signals sit. Their half-minimum imputed values used to mostly track sample depth. Now that detection depth and contamination are regressed out of every protein (round 8) and values are winsorized (round 5), that depth artifact should be mostly gone. I haven't run this, so I don't know the effect on the dev score yet.

I'm adding a biology-based prior to the L2 logistic regression. Proteins already linked to AD in the literature (APOE, CLU, complement C1Q/C3/C4/CFH, A2M, apolipoproteins, acute-phase proteins such as SERPINA3/CHI3L1/HP/CP, TTR/AFM/GSN/PON1, IGFBP2, and leakage markers such as GFAP/NEFL/SMOC1/SPP1) get their final standardized features scaled by 2. That cuts their effective L2 penalty by 4×, so with ~70 samples and ~1,500 proteins the model leans on these markers instead of spreading weight over noise proteins. I haven't run this, so I don't know its effect on the dev score.

Right now each batch's offset is its raw training-fold mean. If AD and control proportions differ between the two batches, that centring removes part of the disease signal along with the technical offset. This change estimates each batch's offset as the average of its within-class means in the training fold, the same idea as including the biological covariate in ComBat's design. If a class has fewer than 2 samples in a batch, or a protein has no observed values for one class, it falls back to the plain batch mean. Test samples are then shifted by these fixed training-fold offsets, so no test labels are used. This hasn't been run, so I don't know its effect on the dev score.

AD-related changes in plasma tend to show up as coordinated shifts across whole pathways: complement activation, changes in lipoprotein/apolipoprotein transport, and positive and negative acute-phase responses. Single protein z-scores are noisy when there are only ~70 training samples. This change adds label-free module scores (the mean of member-protein z-scores, then re-standardized, winsorized and prior-up-weighted ×3) next to the protein features. In the L2 logistic regression this works like a group-structured prior: it lowers the penalty on coherent pathway-level directions, so the model can lean on a pathway's combined evidence instead of a single noisy protein. I haven't run this yet, so I don't know its effect on the dev score.

With about 70 samples and about 1,500 proteins, the L2 logistic regression can still spread weight over correlated noise. A diagonal shrunken-centroid classifier (Tibshirani et al. 2002) ignores covariance, which makes it very stable when p≫n. This change averages its score with the logistic-regression score, so two models with different biases vote. The centroid classifier soft-thresholds per-protein t-statistics computed on the training fold. Both scores are put on a common scale using training-fold statistics, so out-of-fold predictions stay comparable across folds. The prior weights are applied to both models.

Partial clotting during plasma processing is the third contamination axis in Geyer et al. (2019), and it is the one we haven't modelled yet. Clotting uses up fibrinogen, factor XIII, prothrombin and factor V, and how much varies from sample to sample. Regressing out the erythrocyte and platelet panels gave the biggest gain so far (+0.034), so I'm adding a label-free coagulation-consumption score as one more nuisance covariate. Its coefficients are fit on the training fold only. This hasn't been run, and it carries a risk: fibrinogen may itself be linked to AD, so this could remove real signal.

The contamination and detection-depth regression currently fits each protein on `[1, S]` alone, ignoring diagnosis. If haemolysis, platelet or depth scores differ even slightly between AD and controls in the training fold, the nuisance coefficients pick up part of the disease effect, and subtracting them removes real signal. Round 12 fixed this same problem for batch centring and helped. This change adds the training-fold diagnosis to the regression design (ComBat-with-design / RUV-style) and removes only the technical component, so test samples are corrected with the training-fold nuisance coefficients and no test labels.

The C=0.05 setting was carried over from round 1, before contamination/depth regression, winsorization and the biology prior changed the scale of the features. Its best value is now unknown. C is now picked inside each training fold from {0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2} by grouped, stratified inner CV, repeated over 3 shuffles so the choice is less noisy with about 70 samples. One risk: the batch centring uses training labels and is computed once on the full training fold, so the inner-CV scores are slightly optimistic. Inner CV this small is also noisy and could pick a worse C than 0.05.
